outcome: The problem is still open as stated: no accepted proof or disproof of the square case for all Jordan curves has appeared since 26 January 2024. Several in-window arXiv preprints settle the square case for restricted classes (Greene and Lobb, April and July 2024; Asano and Ike, December 2024), and two self-published claims of a full proof (Mu Meson, figshare, January 2025; Ueoka, Zenodo, November 2025) have no visible expert check.
problem_asks: (1) For every Jordan curve in the Euclidean plane (a continuous, injective, closed curve; the Wikipedia wording 'every Jordan curve' imposes no regularity), (2) there exist four points on the curve that are the vertices of a square (a non-degenerate square). The statement asks for existence only; it does not ask for a count or uniqueness of such squares, and the square need not lie inside the curve. Aliases used in the literature: square peg problem, inscribed square problem, Toeplitz's conjecture (Toeplitz 1911). Note that 'Toeplitz conjecture' is also used for unrelated problems (e.g. Toeplitz's inscribed-ellipse problem; Toeplitz matrix questions).

events.what_happened: Meyerson (Fundamenta Mathematicae 110, 1980, 'Equilateral triangles and continuous curves') shows that every Jordan curve inscribes a triangle similar to any given triangle. Different question: three vertices, triangles. Source: the Open Problem Garden page's reference list and summary (opened); the journal article itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Three points forming a triangle similar to any prescribed triangle, on every Jordan curve. No square.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks: the four-vertex square claim is untouched.

checked_by.what_they_did: published the paper (cited as such on the Open Problem Garden page; the article was not opened)

events.direction: Existence result for triangles. Different question from the square case; recorded as a neighbouring result.

events.what_happened: Emch (American Journal of Mathematics, 1916) proves the square case for piecewise analytic curves with finitely many inflection points, including all polygons, per the Open Problem Garden summary (opened). Emch's earlier convex (1913) and smooth-enough (1915) results appear only in search summaries of Matschke's survey and were not opened.
events.delivers: Four vertices of a square on piecewise analytic Jordan curves (finitely many inflection points, per search summary). Covers all polygons.
events.remains: General Jordan curves, including smooth curves that are not piecewise analytic, and continuous curves generally.

checked_by.what_they_did: published the paper (cited on the Open Problem Garden page; the article was not opened)

events.direction: Yes, for a restricted class (piecewise analytic curves).

events.what_happened: Schnirelman (Shnirel'man / Schnirelmann), smooth Jordan curves: the square case, published in Uspekhi Mat. Nauk in 1944 per the Open Problem Garden summary (opened). Some sources date the underlying work to 1929; I record the published date because the 1929 argument is not shown to have been public in writing. Dates disputed; see disputes.
events.revisions: Some sources give 1929 for the original work; the 1944 publication is described as an extended and corrected version.
events.delivers: Four vertices of a square on smooth Jordan curves (the class described in Pak's notes as continuous curvature of bounded variation, slightly larger than C², per search summary).
events.remains: Non-smooth Jordan curves; the general problem.

checked_by.what_they_did: published the result (per the Open Problem Garden summary; the article was not opened)

events.direction: Yes, for smooth curves.

events.what_happened: Vaughan's argument (c. 1977) that every Jordan curve inscribes a rectangle, first published in 1981 in Meyerson's Topology Proceedings write-up, per the Open Problem Garden summary (opened). Different question: rectangles of unspecified aspect ratio, not squares.
events.delivers: Four points forming some rectangle (aspect ratio not fixed) on every Jordan curve.
events.remains: The square case (aspect ratio 1), and every prescribed aspect ratio.

checked_by.what_they_did: published the write-up (per the Open Problem Garden summary; the article was not opened)

events.direction: Existence for rectangles of unspecified shape. Different question from the square case.

events.what_happened: Stromquist, 'Inscribed squares and square-like quadrilaterals in closed curves' (Mathematika 36, 1989, pp. 187–197): the square case for locally monotone curves (every point has a neighbourhood on which some linear function of the curve is monotone), and a weaker sufficient condition covering convex curves, polygons and some piecewise C¹ curves. Known from the Open Problem Garden page (opened, cites the 1989 paper for the C¹ case), the Wikipedia summary (opened), and search summaries of the paper and Matschke's survey. The paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Four vertices of a square on locally monotone Jordan curves (includes polygons, convex curves and piecewise smooth curves without cusps, per search summary).
events.remains: Continuous Jordan curves outside the locally monotone class and the weaker condition.

checked_by.what_they_did: published the paper (per the Cambridge listing in search results; not opened)

events.direction: Yes, for a restricted class (locally monotone curves).

events.what_happened: Matschke, 'On the Square Peg Problem and Its Relatives' (arXiv:1001.0186; v1 submitted 31 Dec 2009; v2 revised 18 Mar 2022, marked accepted version). Proves the square peg problem for several new open classes of curves, one of them dense, and states that the problem is therefore solved for generic curves; also results on rectangles inscribed in immersed curves, and a topological counterexample for regular octahedra on metric 2-spheres. Classes are not named in the abstract read.
events.delivers: Four vertices of a square for several new classes of continuous curves (not named in the abstract), including a dense class that the author describes as covering generic curves. Class definitions were not read.
events.remains: Curves outside those classes, i.e. the general continuous case.
events.direction: Yes, for a dense class of curves; not the full problem.

events.what_happened: Tao, 'An integration approach to the Toeplitz square peg problem' (arXiv:1611.07441; v1 22 Nov 2016; v2 7 Jun 2017, revised per referee suggestions; published Forum of Mathematics, Sigma 5 (2017) e30 per search result). Adds integrals associated to the curve to the homological approach; gives positive answers for curves that are the union of two Lipschitz graphs f, g on [t0, t1] agreeing at the endpoints with Lipschitz constants strictly below one. Also proposes a periodic variant and a combinatorial conjecture on sign patterns of y1+y2+y3.
events.revisions: v1 22 Nov 2016; v2 7 Jun 2017 (revised per referee suggestions).
events.delivers: Squares on Jordan curves formed as the union of two Lipschitz graphs with Lipschitz constants strictly below one, agreeing at the endpoints.
events.remains: Curves not of that form, including Lipschitz constant one or above; the general problem.

checked_by.qualification: journal of record; the arXiv comment says the paper was revised according to referee suggestions
checked_by.what_they_did: refereed and published (2017, vol. 5, e30; per search result, journal page not opened)

events.direction: Yes, for a restricted class (two-graph curves with Lipschitz constant below one).

events.what_happened: Feller and Golla, 'Non-orientable slice surfaces and inscribed rectangles' (arXiv:2003.01590; v1 3 Mar 2020; v2 11 Apr 2021). Main subject is non-orientable slice genera of torus and 2-bridge knots. The abstract states that the approach unifies the existence of inscribed squares and of inscribed rectangles with aspect ratio √3 for Jordan curves with a regularity condition, generalizing Hugelmeyer's smooth-curve result.
events.revisions: v1 3 Mar 2020; v2 11 Apr 2021 ('clearer exposition and improved results in sec 5', per arXiv comment).
events.delivers: Inscribed squares for Jordan curves meeting the paper's regularity condition. A search summary says that condition is locally 1-Lipschitz; the abstract page does not confirm this.
events.remains: Jordan curves that fail the regularity condition; the general problem.
events.direction: Yes, for a restricted (regular) class.

events.what_happened: Greene and Lobb, 'The Rectangular Peg Problem' (arXiv:2005.09193; submitted 19 May 2020). For every smooth Jordan curve and every rectangle, a similar rectangle has its vertices on the curve; proof via Shevchishin's theorem on the Klein bottle and Lagrangian embeddings in C². Published in Annals of Mathematics 194(2), 2021, per search result (journal page not opened). Squares are a special case for smooth curves, which Schnirelman's result already covered. The Open Problem Garden 'already solved' tag (2021) cites this paper.
events.delivers: Rectangles of every shape (including squares) inscribed in every smooth Jordan curve.
events.remains: Non-smooth Jordan curves, i.e. the general problem.

checked_by.what_they_did: published 2021, per search result (journal page not opened)

events.direction: Yes, for smooth curves and all rectangles (squares are a special case).

events.what_happened: Greene and Lobb, 'Cyclic quadrilaterals and smooth Jordan curves' (arXiv:2011.05216, posted 2020; exact day not confirmed). Every smooth Jordan curve inscribes every cyclic quadrilateral. Published Inventiones Mathematicae 234(3) (2023), pp. 931–935, per search result. Squares are cyclic quadrilaterals, so smooth squares are covered. The arXiv page was not opened; this is from a search summary.
events.delivers: Every cyclic quadrilateral (squares included) inscribed in every smooth Jordan curve.
events.remains: Non-smooth Jordan curves; the general problem.
events.direction: Yes, for smooth curves (squares are a special case).

events.what_happened: Fung, 'Every Jordan curve inscribes uncountably many rhombi' (arXiv:2010.05101; submitted 10 Oct 2020; published Geometriae Dedicata 2021 per the arXiv page). No regularity assumed. Different question: rhombi, which are not squares unless their diagonals are equal.
events.delivers: Uncountably many rhombi inscribed in every Jordan curve. Says nothing about squares.
events.remains: The square case; rhombi with equal diagonals.

checked_by.what_they_did: published 2021, per the arXiv page (not opened)

events.direction: Existence for a different shape (rhombi). Recorded as a neighbouring result.

events.what_happened: Cantarella, Denne and McCleary, 'Square-like quadrilaterals inscribed in embedded space curves' (arXiv:2103.13848; submitted 25 Mar 2021). Proves that every embedded space curve of finite total curvature without cusps has an inscribed square-like quadrilateral (equal sides and equal diagonals; in the plane this is a square). The abstract says the square-peg problem is open for continuous Jordan curves and is resolved for regularity classes between continuous and C¹. An AMS abstract from 2006 by the same group is reported in search results but was not opened; the 2021 arXiv write-up is dated here.
events.delivers: Square-like quadrilaterals (squares, when the curve is planar) on embedded curves of finite total curvature without cusps; the abstract states the square case is resolved for regularity classes between continuous and C¹.
events.remains: Continuous Jordan curves outside that class; the general problem.
events.direction: Yes, for a restricted class (finite total curvature, no cusps).

events.what_happened: Chambers, 'On the square peg problem' (arXiv:2203.02613; submitted 4 Mar 2022, single version). If a Jordan curve gamma is close to a C² Jordan curve beta (a map f from gamma's image to beta's image moves points by less than 1/(10κ), κ the maximum unsigned curvature of beta, and f∘gamma has winding number 1), then gamma contains an inscribed square of positive side length.
events.delivers: Squares on Jordan curves in a quantified C⁰-neighbourhood of a C² Jordan curve with winding number one.
events.remains: Jordan curves not close to any C² curve in that sense; the general problem.
events.time_since_posted: about 4.5 years, no expert commentary found in search
events.direction: Yes, for a restricted class (near-C² curves).

events.what_happened: Hugelmeyer, 'Inscribed Squares and Relation Avoiding Paths' (arXiv:2301.01340; submitted 3 Jan 2023, single version). Main theorem: a Jordan curve with no inscribed square would have a structure the author calls a square envelope. Conjectures about relation avoiding paths in complex vector spaces would imply inscribed squares in Jordan curves with finitely many arbitrarily complicated singularities.
events.delivers: A structural reduction: a counterexample to the square case would have to contain a square envelope. A conditional existence result for Jordan curves with finitely many singularities, conditional on conjectures the author does not prove.
events.remains: The square case for all Jordan curves; the conjectures about relation avoiding paths.
events.direction: Conditional: reduction only. No counterexample, no unconditional result.

events.what_happened: Greene and Lobb, 'Floer homology and square pegs' (arXiv:2404.05179; v1 submitted 8 Apr 2024; v2 revised 13 Jul 2024 with updated introduction and streamlined proof of properties of spectral invariants). Constructs a Lagrangian Floer-type homology whose generators are rectangle inscriptions in a real analytic Jordan curve. Spectral invariants show that a rectifiable Jordan curve admits inscriptions of a whole interval of rectangle shapes. The abstract states that such a curve inscribes a square when its enclosed area exceeds half that of a circle of equal diameter. Abstract read via a fetch summary, not verbatim.
events.revisions: v1 8 Apr 2024; v2 13 Jul 2024 (updated introduction; streamlined proof of properties of spectral invariants).
events.delivers: Squares on rectifiable Jordan curves whose enclosed area exceeds half the area of the circle of equal diameter. Rectangles over an interval of shapes for rectifiable curves. The Floer construction itself is stated for real analytic curves; extension to arbitrary curves is by approximation, which the paper does not complete for squares.
events.remains: Rectifiable curves with enclosed area at most half that of the equal-diameter circle; non-rectifiable curves; the general problem.
events.time_since_posted: about 30 months; no expert commentary found, but cited by Barber (2026) as the source of the r = 1/2 rectangle case
events.direction: Yes, for a restricted class (rectifiable curves with area condition).

events.what_happened: Greene and Lobb, 'Square pegs between two graphs' (arXiv:2407.07798; submitted 10 Jul 2024, single version, 28 pp.). Jordan curves formed as the union of two graphs of functions with Lipschitz constant below 1+√2 always inscribe a square; this extends Tao's result for constant below one. At Lipschitz constant exactly one, the curve inscribes rectangles of every similarity class. Method: spectral invariants of Jordan Floer homology under perturbation. Abstract read via a fetch summary, not verbatim.
events.delivers: Squares on Jordan curves that are the union of two graphs with Lipschitz constant below 1+√2. At constant exactly 1: rectangles of every similarity class (whether the square is included at constant 1 is not confirmed on the abstract page).
events.remains: Curves not of two-graph form, or with Lipschitz constant at or above 1+√2; the general problem.
events.time_since_posted: about 27 months; no expert commentary found
events.direction: Yes, for a restricted class (two-graph curves, Lipschitz constant below 1+√2).

events.what_happened: Hugelmeyer, 'A Solution to the Periodic Square Peg Problem' (arXiv:2407.20412; submitted 29 Jul 2024, v1 only; math.SG and math.MG). Resolves the periodic square peg problem by a Lagrangian Floer homology argument: inscribed squares are intersections of two non-displaceable Lagrangians in a symplectic 4-torus. The abstract does not define the periodic problem and does not mention Jordan curves. Tao's 2017 paper describes a periodic variant that remains open even for regular curves; the abstract does not establish whether it is the variant resolved here.
events.delivers: Inscribed squares for the periodic variant, as the abstract describes it. Not a statement about arbitrary Jordan curves as far as the abstract shows.
events.remains: The Toeplitz problem for Jordan curves (unless the periodic variant is identical to it, which is not established).
events.time_since_posted: about 26 months; no expert commentary found
events.direction: Yes, for a periodic variant. Different question unless proved to coincide with the Jordan-curve problem.

events.what_happened: Asano and Ike, 'The rectifiable rectangular peg problem' (arXiv:2412.21057; v1 30 Dec 2024; v2 8 Jun 2025, which per the arXiv comments fixed an error in Section 5; v3 5 Jan 2026, the current version). Abstract: 'We give an affirmative answer to the rectangular peg problem for a large class of continuous Jordan curves that contains all rectifiable curves and Stromquist's locally monotone curves. Our proof is based on microlocal sheaf theory and inspired by recent work of Greene and Lobb.' Theorem 1.1 states the result for every θ in (0, π), a θ-rectangle being one whose diagonals meet at angle θ, provided the curve admits a continuous Legendrian lift (a C⁰ limit of smooth curves with convergent primitives). θ = π/2 is the square case, covered implicitly; the paper does not state squares separately. The introduction, per a fetch summary, calls this the first affirmative answer to the square peg problem for all rectifiable Jordan curves (not checked verbatim).
events.revisions: v1 30 Dec 2024; v2 8 Jun 2025 (fixed an error in Section 5, per arXiv comments); v3 5 Jan 2026 (current).
events.delivers: Squares (θ = π/2 in the rectangle family) inscribed in every continuous Jordan curve that admits a continuous Legendrian lift, a class containing all rectifiable Jordan curves and all of Stromquist's locally monotone curves. For curves in the class, every rectangle angle θ in (0, π) is inscribed.
events.remains: Continuous Jordan curves outside the admitted class (for instance, non-rectifiable curves that are not locally monotone and have no continuous Legendrian lift); the general problem.

checked_by.who: Joshua Evan Greene and Andrew Lobb
checked_by.qualification: authors of the rectangular peg results the paper builds on (Annals 2021; Floer 2024)
checked_by.what_they_did: pointed out an error in an earlier version of the paper, per the authors' acknowledgement; the acknowledgement does not say they checked the current version

events.doubts: The arXiv comments say v2 fixed an error in Section 5 (the Jordan curves section, which contains the main proof). The acknowledgement attributes the report of that error to Greene and Lobb. I did not establish whether the v3 Section 5 is error-free, and I found no independent expert verification. Ike's talks (Tokyo colloquium, 20 June 2025; RIKEN iTHEMS, 17 February 2026) are presentations, not checks. The acknowledgement also says Stéphane Guillermou had proved a similar result; I did not check that result.
events.direction: Yes, for the square case within the admitted class. The square case is implicit in the all-θ theorem rather than stated as its own theorem. Restricted to a class that does not include all continuous Jordan curves.

events.what_happened: A figshare preprint titled 'Inscribed Square Proof', posted under the name 'Mu Meson' on 5 Jan 2025 (per a search excerpt). It claims that every simple closed loop in the plane contains four points forming the vertices of a square. Per the search excerpt, the approach is recursive approximation of loops with mollifiers, Fourier series and wavelets, and uses Brouwer's fixed-point theorem. The figshare page returned HTTP 403 to the fetch tool, the API returned 404, and the DOI redirect led to the same 403, so the record was not read. Date, title and abstract come from search only.
events.delivers: Claimed: the full square problem for every simple closed plane curve. Not checked.
events.remains: Claimed: nothing. Unverified.
events.time_since_posted: about 21 months; no discussion, review or citation found
events.doubts: The author name has no visible mathematical record in any source I could reach, and the record is a single figshare preprint with no journal, referee or expert comment. The proposed route, approximating a Jordan curve by smoother curves and taking a limit of inscribed squares, is the route the Open Problem Garden comments describe as failing, because inscribed squares can shrink to a point in the limit. Whether the preprint handles that gap cannot be checked from the excerpt. The excerpt also includes a remark about natural forms, which is not mathematical evidence.
events.direction: Claims yes, for all Jordan curves. Unverified.
people: 'Mu Meson' (name as shown in the search excerpt; identity not established)

events.what_happened: Zenodo record 17024753, 'Constructive Proof of the Toeplitz Conjecture in R2' (published 1 Sep 2025; a later version v4 is shown; a second work with a fractal-photonic extension is listed on the same record). Single author, self-published. Claims that every simple polygon in R2 with n ≥ 3 vertices has an inscribed ellipse tangent to all side midpoints, by Newton-Raphson iteration, convexity reduction and Banach's fixed-point theorem. Different question: the Toeplitz inscribed-ellipse problem. The shared name is the only link to the square problem. Read via fetch summary.
events.revisions: v4 shown on the record; a newer version is said to exist.
events.delivers: Inscribed ellipses tangent to all side midpoints of simple polygons (claimed). Nothing about squares.
events.remains: Everything asked in problem_asks.
events.direction: Not in the direction of the square question: a different problem that shares the name.
people: Luis Morató de Dalmases (Zenodo record author)

events.what_happened: Zenodo record 17554802 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17554802), 'A Complete Proof of the C⁰ Toeplitz Conjecture: An Approach via the Concept of Permanence and Degree Theory', by Yoshiki Ueoka (sole author, listed as Independent Researcher), published 8 Nov 2025 (created 7 Nov 2025), v1 marked preprint, CC BY 4.0. Per the record's abstract as read through a fetch summary (full PDF restricted), it claims a complete proof for C⁰ Jordan closed curves, relying on Brouwer degree, homotopy invariance and a 'concept of Permanence' proposed by the author, with the argument that the zero set does not vanish under a limit operation. The record's keywords include 'AI-assisted Proof'. Separately, a Medium series under the handle u.yoshiki.phys, which a search summary associates with this author, has posts titled 'The Toeplitz Conjecture: An AI-Human Collaboration to Propose a Solution to the 100-Year-Old Inscribed Square Problem' and 'The Square Peg Solved: A Triumph of Human Insight and AI Logic in the C⁰ Toeplitz Conjecture'. Per search excerpts only (the Medium pages returned HTTP 403), these name Gemini as a collaborator, describe a degree-theory argument for the square case, and say the conjecture is solved for C⁰ curves; the post dates are not known.
events.revisions: v1 Nov 2025 (preprint). The record notes a newer version exists; its number and date are not shown.
events.delivers: Claimed: squares inscribed in every C⁰ Jordan closed curve, i.e. the full square problem. The theorem statement and proof are not visible on the record page; not checked.
events.remains: Claimed: nothing. Unverified.
events.time_since_posted: about 11 months; no referee, journal, expert or public comment found
events.doubts: Self-published, unreviewed preprint; the author is listed as independent, and the Medium excerpts describe the author as having little prior background in topology (per search summary). The record shows 497 views and 194 downloads and no comments. The key step, as the abstract describes it, is a degree argument that the zero set survives a limit operation, which is the approximation-limit step that Open Problem Garden comments say defeats the approximation route, because inscribed squares can shrink to points. The abstract does not show how degenerate squares are excluded, and the full text is restricted. The Medium excerpts describe the argument only at a high level.
events.direction: Claims yes, for every continuous Jordan curve; settles the problem in the direction the conjecture asserts, if correct. Unverified.
people: Yoshiki Ueoka (sole author of the Zenodo record)

sources: https://medium.com/feed/@u.yoshiki.phys (feed opened; the Toeplitz posts are not in the feed)

events.what_happened: Greene and Lobb, 'Jordan curves inscribe a positive measure of rectangles' (arXiv:2604.17116; submitted 18 Apr 2026, v1 only). For an arbitrary Jordan curve of diameter 2R enclosing area A, there is a set I of diagonal angles θ in (0, π) with measure at least A/R² such that for each θ in I the curve has four points at the vertices of a rectangle whose diagonals meet at angle θ. Abstract read via a fetch summary.
events.delivers: For every Jordan curve (no regularity assumption), a positive-measure set of rectangle diagonal angles, with measure at least A/R², that are inscribed.
events.remains: Whether π/2 (squares) lies in I, which the abstract does not state; the square problem in full.
events.direction: Yes, for a positive-measure set of rectangles in every Jordan curve. Squares not established.

events.what_happened: Barber, 'Inscriptions of Isosceles Trapezoids in Jordan Curves' (arXiv:2604.27717; submitted 30 Apr 2026, single version). Builds a Lagrangian Floer homology generated by inscribed isosceles trapezoids (defined in the paper as quadrilaterals whose vertices are the intersection of two parallel lines with a circle). Restates that every smooth Jordan curve inscribes every isosceles trapezoid (Greene–Lobb's result as Theorem 1.3). Uses spectral invariants for new non-smooth cases (Theorem A: locally Lipschitz-graphical curves, r ≠ 1/2, with an angle bound involving enclosed area and radius; Theorem B: rectifiable or locally monotone curves under a non-vanishing spectral condition). Cites Asano–Ike for rectangles of every aspect ratio on rectifiable and locally monotone curves (Theorem 1.5). Read in two fetch passes (the second excerpt stopped before the acknowledgements; theorem statements A and B were taken from the first pass and are not verbatim).
events.delivers: Isosceles trapezoids, with aspect ratio r and angle θ, on new non-smooth classes: locally Lipschitz-graphical curves for r ≠ 1/2 under an area-dependent angle bound (Theorem A), and rectifiable or locally monotone curves under a spectral non-vanishing condition (Theorem B). The rectangle case r = 1/2 is attributed to Greene–Lobb 2024. Squares are not named, and the paper does not say whether they are covered.
events.remains: Square inscription for general Jordan curves; non-smooth curves outside Theorems A and B; any explicit square statement.
events.direction: Yes, for a generalization to isosceles trapezoids on restricted classes. Square case not stated.

events.what_happened: Morales-Fuentes and Villanueva-Segovia, 'Plane separating continua inscribe rectangles' (arXiv:2609.25574; submitted 22 Sep 2026, v1 only). Abstract: if X is a plane separating continuum, then every embedding of X into R² contains the vertices of a Euclidean rectangle; extends Vaughan's Jordan-curve rectangle result via shape theory and Steenrod homology. Different question: rectangles of unspecified shape, not squares. Abstract read via fetch summary.
events.delivers: Some rectangle (any aspect ratio) on every embedding of a plane separating continuum, which includes Jordan curves.
events.remains: Squares; prescribed aspect ratios; the square problem.
events.direction: Different question (rectangles of unspecified shape). Existence-type.

disputes.summary: The Open Problem Garden page tags the problem 'Already solved' (comment of 25 Feb 2021), citing arXiv:2005.09193, which is Greene and Lobb's smooth-curve rectangle paper. The same page's comments say the general case is open and that the C¹ case is known. The Formal Conjectures Lean file also cites 2005.09193 as a reference. The tag is treated here as unreliable.
Schnirelman's smooth-curve result is dated 1929 by some sources and 1944 (publication) by others. The Popular Mechanics and Quanta-derived summaries and Pak's notes differ on this. I record 1944.

The 2021 Popular Mechanics piece (reprinted on Magzter; search result only) is headlined 'Two mathematicians just solved a century old geometry problem', but its text says the Toeplitz proof still eludes experts. The 2020 Quanta headline 'cracks old problem about rectangles' concerns rectangles. Neither is a resolution of the square problem.

The Ueoka Zenodo record (8 Nov 2025) claims a complete proof for C⁰ Jordan curves. The arXiv literature as read (Cantarella–Denne–McCleary 2021; Greene–Lobb 2024; Asano–Ike, Barber, Greene–Lobb 2026) and the Wikipedia summary still state the continuous case as open. The Mu Meson figshare preprint (5 Jan 2025) claims the full problem; the same status conflict applies.

summary: Nothing accepted has changed the status of the square problem for all Jordan curves. Every source I could read (the Wikipedia summary, the Open Problem Garden page, the Greene–Lobb and Barber 2026 preprints, the Asano–Ike v3 and the Tokyo seminar listing) still calls it open. In the window there are five arXiv results with a bearing on squares, of different reach. Greene–Lobb (8 Apr 2024, 'Floer homology and square pegs') gives squares on rectifiable curves whose enclosed area exceeds half that of the equal-diameter disc. Greene–Lobb (10 Jul 2024, 'Square pegs between two graphs') gives squares for two-graph curves with Lipschitz constant below 1+√2. Asano–Ike (30 Dec 2024; v3 5 Jan 2026) states an affirmative answer for every rectangle angle θ in (0, π), squares included, on a class containing all rectifiable and all locally monotone continuous Jordan curves; this is the broadest square-case statement I found, and it is restricted to that class. Greene–Lobb (18 Apr 2026) gives a positive-measure set of rectangles for every Jordan curve but does not say whether π/2 is in that set. Barber (30 Apr 2026) gives isosceles trapezoids on new non-smooth classes and does not address squares. Two self-published claims of a full proof are on record and neither has been checked by anyone I could find. Ueoka (Zenodo, 8 Nov 2025) claims all continuous Jordan curves; a Medium series under a handle that a search summary associates with the same author names Gemini as a collaborator, but I could read those posts only through search excerpts because the Medium pages returned HTTP 403. Mu Meson (figshare, 5 Jan 2025) claims all simple closed curves; its abstract is known only through a search excerpt because the figshare page returned HTTP 403 to every route I tried. No expert engagement with either claim was found. Close calls: (a) whether Asano–Ike is a resolution or a restricted-class result: I record it as restricted, because its square case is implicit in the θ-range and the class is not all Jordan curves; (b) whether Asano–Ike supersedes Greene–Lobb's April 2024 result: for rectifiable curves Asano–Ike is stronger on the square case, but the Greene–Lobb result was an earlier, separate event, so both are recorded; (c) whether Barber's trapezoid theorems reach squares: the paper's parameter r = 1/2 is rectangles and squares are never named; (d) the Ueoka and Mu Meson claims, recorded as unverified claims with the reasons for doubt. The Morató de Dalmases Zenodo record (1 Sep 2025) uses the name 'Toeplitz Conjecture' but concerns inscribed ellipses in polygons, a different problem. The 2021 Open Problem Garden 'already solved' tag points to a smooth-curve rectangle paper, not a resolution. Other older results are in the events: Emch, Schnirelman, Stromquist, Matschke (whose v1 is dated 31 Dec 2009), Tao, Feller–Golla, Greene–Lobb 2020 (smooth rectangles and cyclic quadrilaterals), Cantarella–Denne–McCleary, Chambers and Hugelmeyer 2023. AI screen: I searched for AI involvement with this problem through lab announcements, AI-math trackers and the Formal Conjectures repository. The AI results I found concern other problems (the May 2026 OpenAI unit-distance counterexample; AlphaEvolve packing problems; Harmonic's Aristotle; an Epoch problem credited to a human team and Claude). The only AI-linked claims on this problem are the Ueoka claim (keyword 'AI-assisted Proof' on the record, Gemini named only in Medium excerpts) and the Medium posts. I did not record AI systems in ai.systems for Ueoka, because I could not read the authors' sentence naming Gemini verbatim. Formal Conjectures' InscribedSquare.lean states the problem as 'research open' and lists theorems, including the C² square theorem, with sorry proofs; it is a statement benchmark, not a machine-checked result. Dating notes: Schnirelman is recorded at 1944 (see disputes). Greene–Lobb's cyclic quadrilateral paper is recorded at year 2020 because I did not open the arXiv page.
competing_reading: Asano and Ike's theorem, as read through the arXiv HTML, proves the square case for every rectifiable and every locally monotone continuous Jordan curve (with a continuous Legendrian lift). Rectifiable curves are a large class, and the paper is the broadest square-case result in the window. A reader who counts restricted-class square theorems as movement in the quantity the problem asks for would record in-window movement in December 2024, and would also count the April and July 2024 Greene–Lobb results. The strongest case in the other direction is that every one of these is restricted, the problem asks about all Jordan curves, and nothing in the window has been accepted for the general case. On the claims: if the Ueoka preprint is correct, it settles the whole problem in the direction the conjecture asserts, and it is the event that would change the status. The reason to discount it now is the lack of any visible check and the approximation-limit gap that the Open Problem Garden comments describe for this problem. The Mu Meson preprint is similar but less developed, and its approach has the same gap.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The Asano–Ike paper's Section 5 in v3, with its square-case statement (θ = π/2) written out, and any expert verification of it. (2) The full Ueoka text (Zenodo restricted; the abstract shows no theorem), in particular how the degree argument excludes shrinking squares in the limit, and whether an expert engages with it. (3) The Medium posts, read verbatim: their dates, and the author's own sentence about what Gemini did. (4) The figshare 'Inscribed Square Proof' PDF, its method, and any statement about AI use. (5) Whether Greene–Lobb's April 2026 positive-measure paper includes π/2 in the set I. (6) The full Epoch FrontierMath open-problems list, which I saw only partially (10 of 49 visible), and the full Formal Conjectures listing. (7) Expert commentary on any of the above, e.g. MathOverflow or the arXiv comment fields.

event.what_happened: Greene and Lobb, 'Floer homology and square pegs' (arXiv:2404.05179; v1 submitted 8 Apr 2024; v2 revised 13 Jul 2024 with updated introduction and streamlined proof of properties of spectral invariants). Constructs a Lagrangian Floer-type homology whose generators are rectangle inscriptions in a real analytic Jordan curve. Spectral invariants show that a rectifiable Jordan curve admits inscriptions of a whole interval of rectangle shapes. The abstract states that such a curve inscribes a square when its enclosed area exceeds half that of a circle of equal diameter. Abstract read via a fetch summary, not verbatim.
event.revisions: v1 8 Apr 2024; v2 13 Jul 2024 (updated introduction; streamlined proof of properties of spectral invariants).
event.delivers: Squares on rectifiable Jordan curves whose enclosed area exceeds half the area of the circle of equal diameter. Rectangles over an interval of shapes for rectifiable curves. The Floer construction itself is stated for real analytic curves; extension to arbitrary curves is by approximation, which the paper does not complete for squares.
event.remains: Rectifiable curves with enclosed area at most half that of the equal-diameter circle; non-rectifiable curves; the general problem.
event.time_since_posted: about 30 months; no expert commentary found, but cited by Barber (2026) as the source of the r = 1/2 rectangle case
event.direction: Yes, for a restricted class (rectifiable curves with area condition).

judgement.why: The statement asks whether every Jordan curve inscribes a square, so square theorems for restricted curve classes (Greene–Lobb 2024 Floer and two-graph papers, Asano–Ike rectifiable/locally monotone) are cases, unreviewed but by established researchers with credible methods; Asano–Ike's earlier error was reported by Greene–Lobb and fixed in v2, with no unanswered error, so it stays credible. Results on rectangles of unspecified or measure-many shapes, rhombi, triangles, trapezoids without a stated square case, the periodic variant, and the Toeplitz ellipse problem are variants. Hugelmeyer 2023 is a conditional reduction (none). The two self-published full-proof claims (Mu Meson, Ueoka) combine several F10 signals — outsider authors, no uptake on a landmark problem, later specialist papers still calling it open, and the known-failing approximation-limit method — so both are not_credible. Ueoka's Gemini link is not in ai.systems (excerpts only) and none_found is false, so its AI role is none.
judgement.doubts: Ueoka's AI role rests on unread Medium posts naming Gemini as collaborator; if read verbatim they might support 'assisted', but the event is set aside as not_credible either way. Asano–Ike's square case is implicit (θ = π/2) and v3 Section 5 was not independently verified. Greene–Lobb 2026 might include π/2 in its angle set; if so it would be a case, not a variant.
